summary:
Mizoram stands under India's national framework, which applies directly to the state. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the amendment removes self-identification, requires medical certification for identity recognition, and reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had recognised gender identity on the applicant's own assertion. The same report records new offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone into being transgender, which Human Rights Watch warns could criminalise the support networks trans people rely on. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill.

BBC reporting of 26 March 2026 states that recognition now rests on biological or physical traits alongside traditional identities, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback against the 2014 ruling. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Welfare administration for trans residents varies sharply between Indian states. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, surgery and pensions, while Mizoram's own arrangements are not described in the sources assembled here. A visitor should not assume facilities available in Chennai or Thiruvananthapuram exist in Aizawl.

Official and independent assessments of police conduct do not align. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note characterises police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and non-systemic, whereas victim interviews documented in June 2024 describe abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police, and separate accounts concern custody treatment by the Railway Protection Force in Assam.

Government and activist framings of the March 2026 amendment conflict directly. The government describes the narrower definition as a route to widening welfare coverage and anti-trafficking protection; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mizoram seeking legal recognition of gender identity now face medical certification rather than self-declaration, with certification handled through medical boards and district authorities before gender-affirming surgery can be recognised. Only about 32,500 of the 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census hold identity cards, so document access is already thin across the country.

The new offences for coercing or alluring a person into being transgender fall on families, friends and community organisations as well as on outsiders, and Human Rights Watch warns they could criminalise support networks that trans residents depend on.

Transition-related healthcare is covered nationally under the Ayushman Bharat scheme, expanded in April 2024 to all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Police forces are subject to the sensitisation and protection directions issued by the Madras High Court on 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, and conversion therapy is barred both by that judgment and by the National Medical Commission's 2022 order, though clandestine networks continue to operate.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources assembled here contain no reporting on Mizoram's own police conduct toward trans people, no account of a state welfare board or public surgical facilities in Mizoram, and no evidence on the incidence of conversion therapy within the state. These remain unresolved rather than absent.

Population figures for transgender people in India are not reconciled across sources: the census records 487,803 transgender persons while other reporting estimates around two million. The gap is unexplained in the material available.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill had not received presidential assent as of late March 2026, so its final status and any subsequent judicial challenge are unresolved.

Whether the sexual-violence provisions omitted from the Bharatiya Sanhita will be restored or replaced, and how the new life-imprisonment offences will be charged in practice, are not addressed by the available sources.
